passages.t: What is vine wood good for?
passages.happening:
God asks Ezekiel a question about a vine. ‘Son of man, how does the wood of the vine surpass any other branch among the trees in the forest?’ (verse 2). Can it be made into something useful, even a peg to hang a pot on? (verse 3). No, it is thrown into the fire for fuel. ‘The fire devours both ends, and the middle is charred’ (verse 4). If it was useless whole, how much less when it is burned (verse 5)?

So God will give up the people of Jerusalem like vine wood to the fire. ‘Though they may have escaped the fire, yet another fire will consume them’ (verse 7), and the land will be made desolate because they have been unfaithful (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The vine was one of Israel's most important crops, and it became a picture of Israel itself. Psalm 80 calls Israel a vine God brought out of Egypt, and Isaiah sings of a vineyard that produced only bad grapes. The people of Jerusalem would have heard the image with pride.

But the value of a vine is its fruit. Vine wood is soft, twisted and thin, unlike oak or cedar. It cannot be used for building or tools, and pruned branches were gathered and burned.

Those who ‘escaped the fire’ were probably the people left in Jerusalem after the deportation of 597 BC, who thought of themselves as survivors and perhaps as favored. Ezekiel says the city is already burned at both ends, and another fire is coming.
passages.later: The psalm says of Israel, ‘You uprooted a vine from Egypt’ (Psalm 80:8). Isaiah's song asks, ‘Why, when I expected sweet grapes, did it bring forth sour fruit?’ (Isaiah 5:4).
passages.hard:
Is it fair to call God's people useless, as if their only value were what they produce?

The parable is blunt, and readers who have been told they were worthless may hear it painfully. It helps to see what it is aimed at. Ezekiel speaks to a proud city that believed its chosen status made it safe whatever it did. The parable does not say that people are valuable only for what they produce. It says that Israel's special standing rested on its calling to be faithful, and that calling had been abandoned.

Elsewhere Ezekiel insists that God takes no pleasure in anyone's death (18:32), and he promises a new heart and a restored people (chapters 11, 36 and 37). The parable humbles pride. It is not a verdict on anyone's worth.
passages.asks: The vine's pride was in being chosen, not in bearing fruit. Ask where you rely on your standing with God rather than on walking with him. And ask what fruit he is looking for in your life now.
